title: Ellingham and Pourbaix Diagrams: Metal Stability in Gases and Water
subtitle: How the Gibbs energy of oxidation, plotted against temperature or against potential and pH, governs both the extraction of metals and their corrosion.
excerpt: The Ellingham and Pourbaix diagrams map where a metal is thermodynamically stable, in high-temperature gases and in water. This article explains both, with interactive models.
abstract: Ellingham and Pourbaix diagrams are two projections of the Gibbs energy of metal oxidation. The Ellingham diagram plots ΔG° per mole of O₂ against temperature; slopes set by the change in gas moles explain why carbon reduces wüstite above about 750 °C but alumina only near 2,050 °C, and its gas-ratio scales give the compositions a furnace must hold. The Pourbaix diagram plots electrode potential against pH at 25 °C through ΔG = −nFE, dividing the plane into immunity, corrosion and passivation fields. At 25 °C the two are linked exactly: an Ellingham value converts to the oxide/metal potential at pH 0 as E° = (ΔG° + 474 kJ)/4F.
